A small estimation-to-design example

One biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) model runs through parameter estimation, uncertainty analysis, and experimental design. The complete Pyomo model, calculations, and diagnostics remain together so that a later step uses the results of the earlier fit.

Part I: parameter estimation and local uncertainty. Specify the measurement model, derive the likelihood, fit the data, differentiate the predictions, and construct the local confidence ellipse.

Part II: nonlinear uncertainty and experimental design. Compare likelihood-ratio regions, bootstrap fits, and profiles; choose a new measurement time; then measure, append the data, and refit. The two larger reaction-kinetics tutorials apply the same workflow to dynamic models.

The historical data, the assumed measurement-error model, and the digital experiment serve different roles. The six historical observations determine the initial fit. The known standard deviation of 1 mg/L is an illustrative assumption. The digital experiment supplies new simulated measurements when testing a design.

Part I: parameter estimation and local uncertainty¶

Model and observations¶

The response model is

y(t;θ)=θ1(1−exp⁡(−θ2t)),y(t;\boldsymbol{\theta})=\theta_1\left(1-\exp(-\theta_2t)\right),y(t;θ)=θ1​(1−exp(−θ2​t)),
(1)

where:

  • θ1\theta_1θ1​ is the long-time asymptote;

  • θ2\theta_2θ2​ is the approach rate; and

  • ttt is the measurement time.

We assume independent measurement noise with known standard deviation σ=1\sigma=1σ=1. In Pyomo’s experiment suffix, measurement_error means standard deviation, not variance or weight.

The legacy code column is named time_days; its values in this BOD example are days.

Time is measured in days, response and asymptote in mg/L, and rate in day−1^{-1}−1. The column and Pyomo component are named time_days consistently. Laky et al. (2026), Section 4.1, Equation (32), gives the same model and units; its two-observation example is different from the six-observation fit here.

Source. This is Bates and Watts’ own BOD example. The six observations below are their Table A1.4 (Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its Applications, Wiley, 1988, p. 270), and the response model above is their Equation (2.8), p. 41. The data are not originally theirs: they reproduce them from Marske (1967), Biochemical Oxygen Demand Data Interpretation Using Sum of Squares Surface, M.S. thesis, University of Wisconsin--Madison (their reference list, p. 339). Each entry is the average of two analyses on one inoculated bottle of stream water. Fitting these six points reproduces their published estimate θ^=(19.143, 0.5311)\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = (19.143,\ 0.5311)θ^=(19.143, 0.5311) with s2=6.498s^2 = 6.498s2=6.498 on four degrees of freedom (Example BOD 4, p. 51) -- which is what the assertion in the estimation cell checks. The same data set reaches this course through parmest’s Rooney--Biegler tutorial problem.

The response printed in Appendix A1.4, p. 270 omits the minus sign in the exponent; Equation (2.8), p. 41 has the decreasing exponential used here. A positive exponent with positive rate would give a negative, decreasing demand and is not the fitted BOD model.

A digital experiment¶

At the end of this notebook we will design a new measurement and then take it. The BOD data set is historical, so there is no seventh flask to go back to. We therefore build a digital experiment: a known ground truth θtrue\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{true}}θtrue plus Gaussian noise, which can be queried at any time we like.

The ground truth is chosen close to the historical fit to illustrate the workflow. This choice does not validate the Gaussian noise model against the historical data.

Two data sets are now in play, and it is worth being blunt about which is which:

  • data -- the real BOD observations. This stays the working data set for every estimate below, so the published numbers do not move.

  • simulated -- six draws from the digital experiment at the same times. It appears once to illustrate the generator and is never used for estimation.

The digital experiment earns its keep in the final section, where it supplies the one new measurement the design step asks for.

# Ground truth for the digital experiment. Deliberately close to the historical
# fit; this illustrates the workflow without validating the noise assumption.
THETA_TRUE = {"asymptote": 19.0, "rate_constant": 0.53}
MEASUREMENT_STD = 1.0


def bod_response(t, theta):
    """Noise-free response y(t) = theta_1 * (1 - exp(-theta_2 * t))."""
    t = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
    return theta["asymptote"] * (1.0 - np.exp(-theta["rate_constant"] * t))


def run_digital_experiment(t, rng):
    """Take one measurement at time t: the true response plus one noise draw."""
    return float(bod_response(t, THETA_TRUE) + rng.normal(0.0, MEASUREMENT_STD))


# A fixed seed makes every number in this notebook reproducible, including the
# new measurement taken after the design step.
calibration_rng = np.random.default_rng(60499)

simulated = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "time_days": data["time_days"],
        "y": [run_digital_experiment(t, calibration_rng) for t in data["time_days"]],
    }
)

# Side by side: the historical measurements and six draws from the simulator.
# Compare them without treating visual similarity as model validation.
data.rename(columns={"y": "y (real)"}).assign(**{"y (digital)": simulated["y"].round(2)})

From a measurement model to weighted least squares¶

For experiment iii, hold the design φi\boldsymbol{\varphi}_iφi​ fixed and predict mim_imi​ outputs:

y^i=f(φi,θ),Yi=y^i(θ)+εi,εi∼N(0,Σi).\hat{\mathbf y}_i=\mathbf f(\boldsymbol{\varphi}_i,\boldsymbol\theta),\qquad \mathbf Y_i=\hat{\mathbf y}_i(\boldsymbol\theta)+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i,\qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_i).y^​i​=f(φi​,θ),Yi​=y^​i​(θ)+εi​,εi​∼N(0,Σi​).
(2)

The parameter θ∈Θ⊆Rp\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^pθ∈Θ⊆Rp is fixed but unknown. The estimator θ^(Y)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf Y)θ^(Y) is a rule applied to random data; its value for the observations y\mathbf yy is an estimate. Assume independent experiments and known positive-definite Σi\boldsymbol\Sigma_iΣi​ that do not depend on the parameters. Outputs within an experiment may be correlated.

Define ri(θ)=yi−y^i(θ)\mathbf r_i(\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathbf y_i-\hat{\mathbf y}_i(\boldsymbol\theta)ri​(θ)=yi​−y^​i​(θ). The likelihood is a function of the parameters with the observed data held fixed:

L(θ;y)=∏i=1Nexp⁡[−12riTΣi−1ri](2π)mi/2(det⁡Σi)1/2.L(\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf y) =\prod_{i=1}^N \frac{\exp[-\tfrac12\mathbf r_i^T\boldsymbol\Sigma_i^{-1}\mathbf r_i]} {(2\pi)^{m_i/2}(\det\boldsymbol\Sigma_i)^{1/2}}.L(θ;y)=i=1∏N​(2π)mi​/2(detΣi​)1/2exp[−21​riT​Σi−1​ri​]​.
(3)

Taking the negative logarithm turns the product into a sum:

−log⁡L=12∑imilog⁡(2π)+12∑ilog⁡det⁡Σi+12∑iriTΣi−1ri.-\log L =\frac12\sum_i m_i\log(2\pi) +\frac12\sum_i\log\det\boldsymbol\Sigma_i +\frac12\sum_i\mathbf r_i^T\boldsymbol\Sigma_i^{-1}\mathbf r_i.−logL=21​i∑​mi​log(2π)+21​i∑​logdetΣi​+21​i∑​riT​Σi−1​ri​.
(4)

The first two terms are constant in θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ. Thus the maximum likelihood estimate minimizes

ℓ(θ)=12∑iriTΣi−1ri.\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)=\frac12\sum_i \mathbf r_i^T\boldsymbol\Sigma_i^{-1}\mathbf r_i.ℓ(θ)=21​i∑​riT​Σi−1​ri​.
(5)

Here ℓ\ellℓ always means the summed negative log likelihood with parameter-independent constants removed. For diagonal covariance, this is 12∑i,j(rij/σij)2\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(r_{ij}/\sigma_{ij})^221​∑i,j​(rij​/σij​)2. Halving a standard deviation multiplies its weight by four. For the six BOD observations, mi=1m_i=1mi​=1 and σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 mg/L, so

ℓ(θ)=12∑i=16[yi−θ1(1−e−θ2ti)]2/σ2.\ell(\boldsymbol\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^6 [y_i-\theta_1(1-e^{-\theta_2t_i})]^2/\sigma^2.ℓ(θ)=21​i=1∑6​[yi​−θ1​(1−e−θ2​ti​)]2/σ2.
(6)

See Seber & Wild (1989), §2.1.4, p. 27 and §2.2.1, Eqs. (2.45)--(2.46), pp. 32--33; Nocedal & Wright (2006), §10.1, pp. 249--250. The number of Gaussian scalar components is ∑imi\sum_i m_i∑i​mi​; the number of experiments is NNN. These counts coincide in this scalar-output example.

The estimation/design workflow: update the model or carry remaining uncertainty into a decision.

Generate measurements at fixed designs from a shared response model and independent experiment errors.

Known covariance standardizes the residual before its squared length is computed.

Change the likelihood when the error model changes¶

Stack all residuals in r\mathbf rr. If errors across experiments are correlated, use their joint Gaussian covariance Ω≻0\boldsymbol\Omega\succ0Ω≻0:

−log⁡L=ny2log⁡(2π)+12log⁡det⁡Ω+12rTΩ−1r,ny=∑imi.-\log L=\frac{n_y}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol\Omega +\frac12\mathbf r^T\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1}\mathbf r, \qquad n_y=\sum_i m_i.−logL=2ny​​log(2π)+21​logdetΩ+21​rTΩ−1r,ny​=i∑​mi​.
(7)

Off-diagonal blocks describe dependence between experiments; multiplying their marginal densities would discard this dependence. A scalar measurement_error suffix cannot encode a full off-diagonal covariance. Implement the joint likelihood explicitly for such a model.

If Ω\boldsymbol\OmegaΩ depends on an unknown parameter, retain both its log determinant and its inverse in the objective. Minimizing only the weighted residual term can favor artificially large variances. For independent scalar Laplace errors of known scale b>0b>0b>0, the density is exp⁡(−∣ri∣/b)/(2b)\exp(-|r_i|/b)/(2b)exp(−∣ri​∣/b)/(2b), and the parameter-dependent objective is instead ∑i∣ri∣/b\sum_i|r_i|/b∑i​∣ri​∣/b.

If the response model is implicit, share one parameter vector across all experiments and fit states and predictions together:

min⁡θ,{xi,y^i}12∑i(yi−y^i)TΣi−1(yi−y^i)subject toFi(xi,φi,θ,y^i)=0,i=1,…,N,θ∈Θ.\begin{aligned} \min_{\boldsymbol\theta,\{\mathbf x_i,\hat{\mathbf y}_i\}} &\quad\frac12\sum_i(\mathbf y_i-\hat{\mathbf y}_i)^T \boldsymbol\Sigma_i^{-1}(\mathbf y_i-\hat{\mathbf y}_i)\\ \text{subject to}&\quad \mathbf F_i(\mathbf x_i,\boldsymbol\varphi_i,\boldsymbol\theta,\hat{\mathbf y}_i)=\mathbf0, \quad i=1,\ldots,N,\qquad\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta. \end{aligned}θ,{xi​,y^​i​}min​subject to​21​i∑​(yi​−y^​i​)TΣi−1​(yi​−y^​i​)Fi​(xi​,φi​,θ,y^​i​)=0,i=1,…,N,θ∈Θ.​
(8)

A discretized DAE changes the model constraints, while the likelihood still follows from the measurement assumptions. The dynamic ParmEst tutorial uses this pattern. For other error laws, start with the density before choosing a residual norm; see Nocedal & Wright (2006), §10.1 and Seber & Wild (1989), Chapter 2.

Label one experiment¶

Pyomo’s Experiment abstraction uses four local suffixes:

SuffixRole in this example
experiment_outputsmeasured response and observed value
unknown_parametersparameters and nominal values
measurement_errorresponse standard deviation
experiment_inputscandidate measurement time

parmest uses the first three. Pyomo.DoE also needs experiment_inputs.

class BODExperiment(Experiment):
    """One biochemical oxygen demand measurement and its model labels.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : mapping
        Measurement with keys ``time_days`` (day) and ``y`` (mg/L).
    measurement_standard_deviation : float, optional
        Known measurement standard deviation in mg/L; default 1 is illustrative.
    theta : mapping, optional
        Initial or nominal asymptote (mg/L) and rate_constant (1/day).
    design_bounds : tuple, optional
        Lower and upper allowed measurement times, in days.
    """

    def __init__(self, data, measurement_standard_deviation=1.0,
                 theta=None, design_bounds=(0, 10)):
        # Store the measurement, assumed noise, and initial parameter guesses.
        self.data = dict(data)
        self.sigma = measurement_standard_deviation
        self.theta = theta or {"asymptote": 15.0, "rate_constant": 0.5}
        self.design_bounds = design_bounds
        self.model = None

    def get_labeled_model(self):
        """Build and return the cached Pyomo model with four local suffixes."""
        if self.model is not None:
            return self.model
        # Construct the equations, then attach the reusable tool labels.
        m = build_bod_model(self.data, self.theta, self.design_bounds)
        self.model = label_bod_model(m, self.data, self.sigma)
        return self.model
def build_bod_model(data, theta, design_bounds):
    """Construct one response equation with physically consistent units."""
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    # Unknown physical parameters; positivity is enforced by lower bounds.
    m.asymptote = pyo.Var(initialize=theta["asymptote"],
                         bounds=(1e-6, None), units=pyo.units.mg/pyo.units.L)
    m.rate_constant = pyo.Var(initialize=theta["rate_constant"],
                             bounds=(1e-6, None), units=1/pyo.units.day)
    # The input is fixed when fitting data and freed when designing a run.
    m.time_days = pyo.Var(initialize=data["time_days"],
                          bounds=design_bounds, units=pyo.units.day)
    # This variable is the prediction; the observed value is a suffix below.
    m.y = pyo.Var(initialize=data["y"], units=pyo.units.mg/pyo.units.L)
    # Estimation/design tools unfix the appropriate labeled variables.
    for v in (m.asymptote, m.rate_constant, m.time_days):
        v.fix()
    m.response = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.y == m.asymptote *
                                (1 - pyo.exp(-m.rate_constant * m.time_days)))
    return m
def label_bod_model(m, data, sigma):
    """Attach observations, unknowns, noise scale, and design inputs."""
    # Match each predicted output to its measured value.
    m.experiment_outputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
    m.experiment_outputs[m.y] = data["y"]
    # Tell ParmEst which parameters are shared across experiments.
    m.unknown_parameters = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
    for v in (m.asymptote, m.rate_constant):
        m.unknown_parameters[v] = pyo.value(v)
    # Store standard deviations, not variances, in output units (mg/L).
    m.measurement_error = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
    m.measurement_error[m.y] = sigma
    # Tell Pyomo.DoE which experimental input it may choose.
    m.experiment_inputs = pyo.Suffix(direction=pyo.Suffix.LOCAL)
    m.experiment_inputs[m.time_days] = data["time_days"]
    return m

Estimate the parameters¶

Create one experiment per row. The weighted sum of squared errors divides each residual by its measurement standard deviation before squaring.

ParmEst’s covariance interface requires more experiments than unknown parameters. With known noise variance, a full-rank information matrix can mathematically exist even when the two counts are equal; estimating noise from residuals additionally needs residual degrees of freedom.

Keep the objective normalization visible¶

SSE_weighted uses a per-experiment contribution 12∑j(rij/σij)2\tfrac12\sum_j(r_{ij}/\sigma_{ij})^221​∑j​(rij​/σij​)2. ParmEst returns its average over experiments:

ℓˉ=ℓ/N,ℓ=Nℓˉ.\bar\ell=\ell/N,\qquad \ell=N\bar\ell.ℓˉ=ℓ/N,ℓ=Nℓˉ.
(9)

Multiplication by the positive constant NNN leaves the fitted parameters unchanged. It does change curvature and likelihood-ratio statistics. This notebook forms nll_hat = len(data) * mean_nll before comparing a likelihood increase with a chi-squared cutoff. SSE instead uses unweighted squared residuals without the factor 1/21/21/2; interpreting its value requires a separate noise-scale calculation.

def estimate_parameters(observations):
    """Fit the BOD model to a table of (time_days, y) rows.

    One `BODExperiment` is created per row. Returns the mean negative log
    likelihood, the fitted parameters, and the local covariance matrix -- everything
    needed both to report a fit and to seed the next experimental design.
    """
    experiments = [BODExperiment(row) for row in observations.to_dict("records")]
    estimator = Estimator(experiments, obj_function="SSE_weighted")

    weighted_sse, theta = estimator.theta_est()
    covariance = np.asarray(estimator.cov_est(method="finite_difference"))
    return weighted_sse, theta, covariance


weighted_sse, theta, covariance = estimate_parameters(data)

standard_deviation = np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
correlation = covariance / np.outer(standard_deviation, standard_deviation)

print(f"Mean half weighted SSE: {weighted_sse:.6f}")
print("Parameters:", theta)
print("Covariance:\n", covariance)
print("Correlation:\n", correlation)

assert np.isclose(theta["asymptote"], 19.1426, rtol=2e-4)
assert np.isclose(theta["rate_constant"], 0.53109, rtol=2e-4)

Sensitivities for explicit and implicit models¶

Stack the predictions in y^∈Rny\hat{\mathbf y}\in\mathbb R^{n_y}y^​∈Rny​ and use a row-oriented Jacobian:

Q=dy^dθ∈Rny×p,Qaj=dy^adθj.\mathbf Q=\frac{d\hat{\mathbf y}}{d\boldsymbol\theta}\in\mathbb R^{n_y\times p}, \qquad Q_{aj}=\frac{d\hat y_a}{d\theta_j}.Q=dθdy^​​∈Rny​×p,Qaj​=dθj​dy^​a​​.
(10)

For BOD, one observation contributes the sensitivity row

q(t)=[1−e−θ2tθ1te−θ2t].\mathbf q(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1-e^{-\theta_2t}&\theta_1t e^{-\theta_2t}\end{bmatrix}.q(t)=[1−e−θ2​t​θ1​te−θ2​t​].
(11)

Both entries vanish at t=0t=0t=0: such a measurement supplies no information about these two parameters under this response model. For large ttt, sensitivity to the asymptote approaches one while sensitivity to the rate tends to zero.

For an implicit model, collect states and predictions in z\mathbf zz and write F(z(θ),φ,θ)=0\mathbf F(\mathbf z(\boldsymbol\theta),\boldsymbol\varphi,\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathbf0F(z(θ),φ,θ)=0. At a solution where F\mathbf FF is continuously differentiable and the square matrix Fz\mathbf F_{\mathbf z}Fz​ is nonsingular, the implicit-function theorem gives a locally unique differentiable solution branch. Differentiating at fixed design gives

FzZ+Fθ=0,Z=dzdθ,FzZ=−Fθ.\mathbf F_{\mathbf z}\mathbf Z+\mathbf F_{\boldsymbol\theta}=\mathbf0, \qquad \mathbf Z=\frac{d\mathbf z}{d\boldsymbol\theta}, \qquad \mathbf F_{\mathbf z}\mathbf Z=-\mathbf F_{\boldsymbol\theta}.Fz​Z+Fθ​=0,Z=dθdz​,Fz​Z=−Fθ​.
(12)

Solve this linear system for the sensitivity columns. If outputs are written separately as y^=h(x,φ,θ)\hat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf h(\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\varphi,\boldsymbol\theta)y^​=h(x,φ,θ), include both paths of parameter dependence:

Q=hθ+hxdxdθ.\mathbf Q=\mathbf h_{\boldsymbol\theta} +\mathbf h_{\mathbf x}\frac{d\mathbf x}{d\boldsymbol\theta}.Q=hθ​+hx​dθdx​.
(13)

Automatic differentiation provides partial derivatives; differentiating through the model also requires the changing states. Forming an explicit matrix inverse is unnecessary. See Biegler (2010), §9.3.1, p. 261, Eqs. (9.21)--(9.22), and the erratum to the output-gradient formula on that page. A missing state/output dependence or a missing minus sign changes the sensitivity.

Total prediction sensitivity includes both direct and solved-state paths.

Differentiate the objective and obtain a Gauss--Newton step¶

Let W=blockdiag⁡(Σ1−1,…,ΣN−1)\mathbf W=\operatorname{blockdiag}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\boldsymbol\Sigma_N^{-1})W=blockdiag(Σ1−1​,…,ΣN−1​) be fixed. Because r=y−y^\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\hat{\mathbf y}r=y−y^​, its Jacobian is −Q-\mathbf Q−Q. For ℓ=12rTWr\ell=\tfrac12\mathbf r^T\mathbf W\mathbf rℓ=21​rTWr,

∇ℓ=−QTWr,∇2ℓ=QTWQ−∑a=1ny(Wr)a∇2y^a.\nabla\ell=-\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf r, \qquad \nabla^2\ell=\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf Q -\sum_{a=1}^{n_y}(\mathbf W\mathbf r)_a\nabla^2\hat y_a.∇ℓ=−QTWr,∇2ℓ=QTWQ−a=1∑ny​​(Wr)a​∇2y^​a​.
(14)

Gauss--Newton drops the residual-weighted output-curvature term. Equivalently, linearize the predictions at the current iterate and solve a weighted linear least-squares problem:

y^(θ+s)≈y^(θ)+Qs,min⁡s12∥W1/2(r−Qs)∥22.\hat{\mathbf y}(\boldsymbol\theta+\mathbf s) \approx\hat{\mathbf y}(\boldsymbol\theta)+\mathbf Q\mathbf s, \qquad \min_{\mathbf s}\frac12\|\mathbf W^{1/2}(\mathbf r-\mathbf Q\mathbf s)\|_2^2.y^​(θ+s)≈y^​(θ)+Qs,smin​21​∥W1/2(r−Qs)∥22​.
(15)

The normal equations and damped update are

(QTWQ)s=QTWr,θ+=θ+αs,0<α≤1.(\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf Q)\mathbf s=\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf r, \qquad\boldsymbol\theta^+=\boldsymbol\theta+\alpha\mathbf s, \qquad0<\alpha\le1.(QTWQ)s=QTWr,θ+=θ+αs,0<α≤1.
(16)

Full column rank makes the normal matrix positive definite. QR or SVD of the whitened Jacobian avoids explicitly forming an inverse and is preferable when conditioning is poor. The approximation is exact for an affine response. At a nonlinear noisy-data fit, stationarity means QTWr=0\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf r=\mathbf0QTWr=0, not that every residual is zero.

For the undamped iteration near a regular stationary solution, smoothness, full rank, and a sufficiently small omitted curvature term give local convergence. With zero residual and a Lipschitz Jacobian, the local rate is quadratic. A nonzero residual generally leaves a linear error term; sufficiently large residual-weighted curvature can prevent even local convergence. These statements require a close starting point and do not establish global convergence. Line searches and trust regions address failures of the full step. See Dennis & Schnabel, §10.2, Theorem 10.2.1 and Corollary 10.2.2, pp. 222--225; Seber & Wild, §2.1.3, pp. 25--27.

The independent BOD calculation below includes the omitted term in the observed Hessian and checks the Gauss--Newton covariance separately.

Gauss–Newton projects the observed response onto the local affine prediction model; the sketch uses an illustrative one-parameter response curve, not BOD data.

Check the covariance implementation¶

For this nonlinear model the inverse observed Hessian need not equal inverse expected information. The analytic calculation below validates the selected finite-difference method.

In the installed course build, cov_est(method="reduced_hessian") returned a matrix differing from the independently differentiated observed Hessian. Its call is shown above for API reference, but it is not used in this design demonstration. The third interface also requires a working k_aug installation. These software options are not interchangeable mathematical definitions.

# Independent checks of the mathematics and objective normalization.
t = data["time_days"].to_numpy(float)
a, k = theta["asymptote"], theta["rate_constant"]
e = np.exp(-k*t)
Q = np.column_stack([1-e, a*t*e])
r = data["y"].to_numpy(float) - a*(1-e)
M = Q.T @ Q  # sigma = 1
H = M.copy()
H[0, 1] -= np.sum(r*t*e)
H[1, 0] = H[0, 1]
H[1, 1] += np.sum(r*a*t*t*e)
assert np.allclose(cov_fd, np.linalg.inv(M), rtol=2e-5, atol=1e-7)
assert np.isclose(nll_hat, 0.5*(r@r), rtol=1e-10)
assert np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ r) < 1e-5
print("Independent inverse observed Hessian:")
print(np.linalg.inv(H))
from pyomo.util.check_units import assert_units_consistent
assert_units_consistent(experiments[0].get_labeled_model())

Expected information and estimator covariance¶

Before collecting data, Y\mathbf YY is random. At a fixed parameter and design, the Gaussian measurement model gives Eθ[r(θ;Y)]=0\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\mathbf r(\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf Y)]=\mathbf0Eθ​[r(θ;Y)]=0. The Jacobian and output Hessians are deterministic at that parameter, so

M(θ)=Eθ[∇2ℓ(θ;Y)]=QTWQ−∑aEθ[(Wr)a]∇2y^a=QTWQ=∑iQiTΣi−1Qi.\begin{aligned} \mathbf M(\boldsymbol\theta) &=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\nabla^2\ell(\boldsymbol\theta;\mathbf Y)]\\ &=\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf Q -\sum_a\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[(\mathbf W\mathbf r)_a]\nabla^2\hat y_a\\ &=\mathbf Q^T\mathbf W\mathbf Q =\sum_i\mathbf Q_i^T\boldsymbol\Sigma_i^{-1}\mathbf Q_i. \end{aligned}M(θ)​=Eθ​[∇2ℓ(θ;Y)]=QTWQ−a∑​Eθ​[(Wr)a​]∇2y^​a​=QTWQ=i∑​QiT​Σi−1​Qi​.​
(17)

This equality is exact for known, parameter-independent Gaussian covariance. It identifies expected Fisher information with the Gauss--Newton matrix, not with every realized observed Hessian. Under regularity conditions, information is also the covariance of the likelihood score. The score has the opposite sign to ∇ℓ\nabla\ell∇ℓ because ℓ\ellℓ is a negative log likelihood. See Held & Sabanés Bové (2014), §4.1.1, p. 81 and §5.4.

An estimator is unbiased if Eθ[θ^]=θ\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}]=\boldsymbol\thetaEθ​[θ^]=θ for every parameter value. It is consistent if θ^N→Pθ\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_N\xrightarrow{P}\boldsymbol\thetaθ^N​P​θ as the sample grows. These are different properties; neither alone guarantees the other.

For an unbiased vector estimator, the Cramér--Rao inequality is

Cov⁡θ(θ^)⪰M(θ)−1.\operatorname{Cov}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) \succeq\mathbf M(\boldsymbol\theta)^{-1}.Covθ​(θ^)⪰M(θ)−1.
(18)

This requires a regular statistical model, differentiation/expectation interchange, finite covariance, and nonsingular information at an interior parameter. The matrix inequality compares variance in every fixed direction. It does not assert that a nonlinear MLE is unbiased at finite sample size. Under appropriate identifiability and large-sample regularity conditions, MLEs are asymptotically normal and efficient. We estimate their covariance by

V^=M(θ^)−1.\widehat{\mathbf V}=\mathbf M(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^{-1}.V=M(θ^)−1.
(19)

This is a local approximation for six BOD observations. Full rank at a fitted point alone does not establish the large-sample assumptions or correct model specification. See Held & Sabanés Bové, §4.2.1, pp. 95--98 and §5.4.2, pp. 144--145; Seber & Wild, Eq. (5.2), p. 191.

What a confidence region covers¶

A confidence procedure produces a random set C1−α(Y)\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}(\mathbf Y)C1−α​(Y). Its coverage at a fixed true parameter is

Pr⁡θ{θ∈C1−α(Y)}.\Pr_{\boldsymbol\theta}\{\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}(\mathbf Y)\}.θPr​{θ∈C1−α​(Y)}.
(20)

The target is 1−α1-\alpha1−α over repeated data sets. The true parameter stays fixed while the estimates and sets change. An observed frequentist confidence region does not assign a posterior probability to the parameter.

The random residual-curvature term averages to zero at the true parameter.

The local fit maps measurement errors into parameter errors; its propagated covariance is inverse information for a full-rank unconstrained affine model.

From standardized errors to a confidence ellipsoid¶

If Z1,…,ZkZ_1,\ldots,Z_kZ1​,…,Zk​ are independent standard normal variables, then S=∑jZj2S=\sum_jZ_j^2S=∑j​Zj2​ has distribution χk2\chi_k^2χk2​, mean kkk, and variance 2k2k2k. Its support is nonnegative. The 95th percentile leaves a 5% upper tail; it is not a normal quantile. See Held & Sabanés Bové, Appendix A.5, p. 337.

For a zero-mean multivariate normal error e=θ^−θ\mathbf e=\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\thetae=θ^−θ with covariance V≻0\mathbf V\succ0V≻0, write V=Udiag⁡(vj)UT\mathbf V=\mathbf U\operatorname{diag}(v_j)\mathbf U^TV=Udiag(vj​)UT, where U\mathbf UU is orthogonal and vj>0v_j>0vj​>0. Rotation and scaling give

u=diag⁡(vj−1/2)UTe,Cov⁡(u)=I,∥u∥22=eTV−1e∼χp2.\mathbf u=\operatorname{diag}(v_j^{-1/2})\mathbf U^T\mathbf e, \qquad\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf u)=\mathbf I, \qquad \|\mathbf u\|_2^2=\mathbf e^T\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf e\sim\chi_p^2.u=diag(vj−1/2​)UTe,Cov(u)=I,∥u∥22​=eTV−1e∼χp2​.
(21)

For a jointly normal vector, uncorrelated components are independent. Uncorrelated nonnormal components need not be independent. Applying the normal approximation to the fitted parameters and replacing V\mathbf VV by its estimate makes this chi-squared calibration approximate.

Ellipsoid axes and the role of noise scale¶

Invert the standardized-distance test to obtain the local region

C1−αW={θ:(θ−θ^)TV^−1(θ−θ^)≤c},c=χp,1−α2.\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm W} =\{\boldsymbol\theta:(\boldsymbol\theta-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^T \widehat{\mathbf V}^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) \le c\},\qquad c=\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}.C1−αW​={θ:(θ−θ^)TV−1(θ−θ^)≤c},c=χp,1−α2​.
(22)

In covariance eigenvector coordinates, the boundary is ∑jwj2/vj=c\sum_j w_j^2/v_j=c∑j​wj2​/vj​=c. Its semi-axis along eigenvector jjj has length cvj\sqrt{cv_j}cvj​​. If V^=M−1\widehat{\mathbf V}=\mathbf M^{-1}V=M−1, the same axis has length c/λj\sqrt{c/\lambda_j}c/λj​​ for the information eigenvalue paired with that eigenvector. Inversion reverses ascending eigenvalue order. A long axis identifies a weakly informed combination in the chosen parameter units.

The ppp-dimensional volume is bpcp/2det⁡V^b_p c^{p/2}\sqrt{\det\widehat{\mathbf V}}bp​cp/2detV​, where bpb_pbp​ is the unit-ball volume. For p=2p=2p=2, the area is πcdet⁡V^\pi c\sqrt{\det\widehat{\mathbf V}}πcdetV​. The axis ratio is affected by parameter units; rescaling axes in a plotting program does not change the statistical construction.

Known versus estimated variance. With a known common σ2\sigma^2σ2, V^=σ2(QTQ)−1\widehat{\mathbf V}=\sigma^2(\mathbf Q^T\mathbf Q)^{-1}V=σ2(QTQ)−1 and the cutoff is χp,1−α2\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}χp,1−α2​. If variance is estimated as s2=SSEmin⁡/(n−p)s^2=\mathrm{SSE}_{\min}/(n-p)s2=SSEmin​/(n−p), the usual linearization region instead has

(θ−θ^)TQTQ(θ−θ^)≤ps2Fp,n−p;1−α.(\boldsymbol\theta-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})^T\mathbf Q^T\mathbf Q (\boldsymbol\theta-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) \le p s^2F_{p,n-p;1-\alpha}.(θ−θ^)TQTQ(θ−θ^)≤ps2Fp,n−p;1−α​.
(23)

This F calibration is exact for a full-rank Gaussian linear model and approximate for nonlinear regression. Bates & Watts, Eq. (2.13), p. 53 and Seber & Wild, Eq. (5.9), p. 194 use this estimated-variance version. Held & Sabanés Bové, §5.4.2, p. 145 gives the multivariate normal/Wald construction. The known-noise BOD ellipse below uses p=2p=2p=2 and c=5.9914645c=5.9914645c=5.9914645; its nominal coverage is not a small-sample guarantee.

Rotate the correlated parameter errors and divide by directional standard deviations before using a central chi-squared cutoff.

def plot_local_ellipse(results):
    """Draw the actual BOD covariance ellipse, with its two semi-axes."""
    center = np.array([results["theta"]["asymptote"], results["theta"]["rate_constant"]])
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(np.asarray(results["covariance"]))
    lengths = np.sqrt(results["cutoff"] * values)
    angle = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 361)
    ellipse = center[:, None] + vectors @ (lengths[:, None] * np.vstack([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)]))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.2))
    ax.plot(*ellipse, color="black", label="Local 95% boundary")
    for j, (color, style) in enumerate([("#0072B2", "--"), ("#D55E00", ":")]):
        ends = center[:, None] + np.outer(vectors[:, j] * lengths[j], [-1, 1])
        ax.plot(*ends, color=color, linestyle=style, linewidth=2,
                label=f"Axis {j+1}")
    ax.plot(*center, "kx", markersize=9, markeredgewidth=2, label="Fitted parameters")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"$\theta_1$ (mg/L)", ylabel=r"$\theta_2$ (day$^{-1}$)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

fig = plot_local_ellipse(results)
helper.save_figure(fig, "bod-local-ellipse")
plt.show()

Part II: nonlinear uncertainty and experimental design¶

Likelihood-ratio regions beyond the ellipse¶

For testing all ppp parameters jointly, compare a candidate with the unrestricted MLE:

Λ(θ0)=L(θ0)L(θ^),D(θ0)=−2log⁡Λ=2[ℓ(θ0)−ℓ(θ^)].\Lambda(\boldsymbol\theta_0)=\frac{L(\boldsymbol\theta_0)}{L(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}, \qquad D(\boldsymbol\theta_0)=-2\log\Lambda =2[\ell(\boldsymbol\theta_0)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})].Λ(θ0​)=L(θ^)L(θ0​)​,D(θ0​)=−2logΛ=2[ℓ(θ0​)−ℓ(θ^)].
(24)

The likelihood-ratio region retains candidates with D≤χp,1−α2D\le\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}D≤χp,1−α2​. It evaluates the nonlinear likelihood, rather than imposing an elliptical shape. The cutoff still relies on regularity and large-sample calibration. With known common σ\sigmaσ, the BOD statistic is

D(θ)=SSE(θ)−SSE(θ^)σ2.D(\boldsymbol\theta) =\frac{\mathrm{SSE}(\boldsymbol\theta)-\mathrm{SSE}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}{\sigma^2}.D(θ)=σ2SSE(θ)−SSE(θ^)​.
(25)

The later comparison plots use the same original fit, the same six observations, and σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 mg/L for both the nonlinear region and the Gauss--Newton ellipse. A joint test fixes both BOD parameters and uses 2 degrees of freedom. A profile test fixes one and reoptimizes the other, so it uses 1. Parameter boundaries, unidentified parameters, or small samples can invalidate the usual chi-squared approximation. See Held & Sabanés Bové, §5.4.4, pp. 146--147, Eq. (5.15).

Why the textbook’s BOD contours are much larger¶

Bates & Watts, Example BOD 4, p. 51 estimates s2=6.498s^2=6.498s2=6.498 on 4 residual degrees of freedom. Its BOD contours in §6.1.1, p. 202 use estimated variance and an F-based construction. They extend to arbitrarily large rate constants. Those contours do not use this notebook’s assumed known σ=1\sigma=1σ=1.

The difference can be checked directly. As θ2→∞\theta_2\to\inftyθ2​→∞, all positive-time responses approach θ1\theta_1θ1​. The best horizontal line is θ1=yˉ\theta_1=\bar yθ1​=yˉ​, with limiting SSE ∑i(yi−yˉ)2≈107.2\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\approx107.2∑i​(yi​−yˉ​)2≈107.2, compared with the nonlinear minimum ≈25.99\approx25.99≈25.99. The known-unit-variance statistic tends to ≈81.21\approx81.21≈81.21, far above the joint 95% cutoff 5.991. The same limiting fit can lie inside the much broader estimated-variance, F-calibrated region. Boundedness is conditional on the error model, noise scale, confidence level, and parameter domain.

Curvature distinguishes bending of the response manifold away from its tangent plane (intrinsic curvature) from distortion of coordinates along that manifold (parameter-effects curvature). Reparametrization can reduce the latter, while intrinsic bending remains. Curvature diagnostics and nonlinear regions help assess the local approximation; a small-looking ellipse by itself does not validate it. See Bates & Watts, Chapter 7, pp. 232, 245--246. No curvature measure is computed by the cells below.

Bootstrap: simulate or resample, then refit¶

A bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution by repeatedly refitting artificial data sets. For the fixed BOD times and assumed known Gaussian noise, use the parametric bootstrap below. A residual bootstrap instead resamples centered residuals at fixed times; a case bootstrap resamples whole (time, response) experiments. These answer different sampling questions.

The 200 replicates are a classroom demonstration, not a precision claim about interval endpoints. Bootstrap intervals are approximate and can be unreliable with six observations. The assumed standard deviation 1 is illustrative; the historical residuals are larger than this noise assumption predicts.

Regression resampling reference: Wehrens, Putter & Buydens (2000), §7.2, pp. 47–48, DOI.

Use fixed-design parametric resampling when the planned times and assumed error law represent the repeated experiment. Case resampling instead redraws complete (time, response) pairs; some times disappear and others repeat. It is appropriate for sampling cases from a population, and need not represent a fixed experimental design. See Wehrens, Putter, and Buydens (2000), Section 7.2, pp. 47–48. The bootstrap cloud estimates sampling variation; it is not itself a calibrated joint confidence region or a Bayesian posterior.

The artificial data and refits¶

First fit the original observations. For bootstrap replicate bbb, keep the planned times and generate independent errors from the assumed measurement model:

yi∗(b)=y^(ti;θ^)+εi∗(b),εi∗(b)∼N(0,σ2),θ^∗(b)∈arg⁡min⁡θ∈Θ12∑i[yi∗(b)−y^(ti;θ)σ]2.y_i^{*(b)}=\hat y(t_i;\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})+\varepsilon_i^{*(b)}, \quad\varepsilon_i^{*(b)}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2), \qquad \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{*(b)}\in\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta} \frac12\sum_i\left[\frac{y_i^{*(b)}-\hat y(t_i;\boldsymbol\theta)}{\sigma}\right]^2.yi∗(b)​=y^​(ti​;θ^)+εi∗(b)​,εi∗(b)​∼N(0,σ2),θ^∗(b)∈argθ∈Θmin​21​i∑​[σyi∗(b)​−y^​(ti​;θ)​]2.
(26)

Use the empirical distribution of these refits to estimate sampling variation. A percentile interval for component jjj is [qα/2(θ^j∗),q1−α/2(θ^j∗)][q_{\alpha/2}(\hat\theta_j^*),q_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat\theta_j^*)][qα/2​(θ^j∗​),q1−α/2​(θ^j∗​)]. Such componentwise intervals are not a simultaneous joint region. More replicates reduce Monte Carlo error, not model misspecification or limitations of six original observations.

For residual resampling with exchangeable homoscedastic errors, center the fitted residuals, sample them with replacement, and add them to the fitted response at each fixed time. Heteroscedastic or dependent errors require an appropriate alternative; blindly resampling a common residual pool discards that structure. Case resampling instead redraws whole experiments, changing which times occur. See Wehrens, Putter & Buydens (2000), §7.2, pp. 47--48. Inspect numerical failures and extreme fits before reporting intervals; do not silently drop them.

Fix the original fit during simulation, then refit every artificial data set.

# Parametric bootstrap: keep times fixed; simulate noise and refit.
rng = np.random.default_rng(804)
bootstrap_theta = []
for b in range(200):
    sample = data.copy()
    sample["y"] = bod_response(data["time_days"], theta) + rng.normal(0, 1, len(data))
    exps = [BODExperiment(row) for row in sample.to_dict("records")]
    fit = Estimator(exps, obj_function="SSE_weighted",
                    solver_options={"linear_solver": "mumps"})
    _, theta_b = fit.theta_est()
    bootstrap_theta.append(dict(theta_b))
bootstrap_theta = pd.DataFrame(bootstrap_theta)
print("Illustrative 95% percentile intervals (200 replicates):")
print(bootstrap_theta.quantile([0.025, 0.975]).round(4).to_string())

Built-in case bootstrap¶

theta_est_bootstrap resamples Experiment objects. It does not implement the fixed-time parametric algorithm above. ParmEst also filters insufficiently diverse resamples; with six observations this distinction matters.

# Resample whole (time, response) experiments; retain sample indices.
case_theta = pest.theta_est_bootstrap(100, seed=804, return_samples=True)
# Extreme values flag fits to inspect, not intervals to trust.
print("Case fits with rate > 10:", int((case_theta["rate_constant"] > 10).sum()))
Case fits with rate > 10: 8

Some case resamples produce extremely large rate estimates. The response becomes nearly saturated at all selected times. This can reflect weak information or a solver stopping at a poor stationary point. Independent checks found lower objective values for several returned fits. A solver reporting convergence does not make a fit reliable. Inspect the fit and try other initial values before constructing intervals; do not silently delete these samples. The fixed-design parametric bootstrap above is a different sampling experiment.

# Diagnose case fits without deleting or replacing samples.
# At fixed rate the least-squares asymptote has a closed-form solution.
poor_fits = 0
for _, fit in case_theta.iterrows():
    sample = data.iloc[fit["samples"]]
    ts, ys = sample["time_days"].to_numpy(), sample["y"].to_numpy()
    returned_sse = np.sum((ys - fit["asymptote"] *
                          (1-np.exp(-fit["rate_constant"]*ts)))**2)
    best_trial = returned_sse
    for trial_rate in (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 2.0):
        basis = 1-np.exp(-trial_rate*ts)
        trial_asymptote = (basis @ ys)/(basis @ basis)
        best_trial = min(best_trial, np.sum((ys-trial_asymptote*basis)**2))
    poor_fits += best_trial < returned_sse - 1e-3
print("Case fits with a demonstrably better feasible point:", poor_fits)
Case fits with a demonstrably better feasible point: 2

Profile likelihood: fix one parameter, refit the others¶

For each trial value ccc of parameter jjj, solve

ℓp,j(c)=min⁡{ℓ(θ):θ∈Θ, θj=c},Dj(c)=2[ℓp,j(c)−ℓ(θ^)].\ell_{p,j}(c)=\min\{\ell(\boldsymbol\theta):\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta,\ \theta_j=c\}, \qquad D_j(c)=2[\ell_{p,j}(c)-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})].ℓp,j​(c)=min{ℓ(θ):θ∈Θ, θj​=c},Dj​(c)=2[ℓp,j​(c)−ℓ(θ^)].
(27)

A conditional slice holds the other parameters fixed. A profile reoptimizes them, so the profile objective cannot exceed the corresponding feasible conditional slice. This distinction captures parameter tradeoffs. A pointwise approximate 95% interval keeps Dj(c)≤χ1,0.952=3.841D_j(c)\le\chi^2_{1,0.95}=3.841Dj​(c)≤χ1,0.952​=3.841; it tests one restriction, not two.

Bates & Watts’ profile sum of squares S~j(c)\widetilde S_j(c)Sj​(c) is not our negative log likelihood. With known common σ\sigmaσ,

ℓp,j(c)=S~j(c)2σ2,Dj(c)=S~j(c)−S(θ^)σ2.\ell_{p,j}(c)=\frac{\widetilde S_j(c)}{2\sigma^2}, \qquad D_j(c)=\frac{\widetilde S_j(c)-S(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}{\sigma^2}.ℓp,j​(c)=2σ2Sj​(c)​,Dj​(c)=σ2Sj​(c)−S(θ^)​.
(28)

Their signed profile ttt function uses estimated residual scale sss:

τj(c)=sign⁡(c−θ^j)S~j(c)−S(θ^)s.\tau_j(c)=\operatorname{sign}(c-\hat\theta_j) \frac{\sqrt{\widetilde S_j(c)-S(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}}{s}.τj​(c)=sign(c−θ^j​)sSj​(c)−S(θ^)​​.
(29)

They compare ∣τj∣|\tau_j|∣τj​∣ with a Student ttt cutoff on n−pn-pn−p degrees of freedom. For nonlinear regression that calibration is nominal, not an exact-coverage theorem. A straight profile ttt plot indicates linear behavior in those coordinates; a profile trace plots the reoptimized nuisance parameters against ccc. See Bates & Watts, §6.1.2, Eqs. (6.3)--(6.4), pp. 205--207.

The stable Pyomo model below uses summed half SSE, the same BOD response, known unit noise, and the positive parameter domain. It supplies all plotted profile results. Extend a grid that lacks a threshold crossing, inspect parameter bounds and solve status, and check alternative starts if a constrained fit finds an objective below the supposed unrestricted minimum. A truncated grid is not evidence of an unbounded interval.

Reference: Raue et al. (2009), pp. 1924--1926.

If the common noise variance is unknown¶

For nnn independent scalar Gaussian errors, keep the variance-dependent term:

ℓ(θ,σ2)=n2log⁡(σ2)+S(θ)2σ2+C.\ell(\boldsymbol\theta,\sigma^2)=\frac n2\log(\sigma^2)+\frac{S(\boldsymbol\theta)}{2\sigma^2}+C.ℓ(θ,σ2)=2n​log(σ2)+2σ2S(θ)​+C.
(30)

At fixed θ\boldsymbol\thetaθ with S(θ)>0S(\boldsymbol\theta)>0S(θ)>0, minimization over variance gives σ^2(θ)=S(θ)/n\hat\sigma^2(\boldsymbol\theta)=S(\boldsymbol\theta)/nσ^2(θ)=S(θ)/n, the ML variance estimate. Substitution gives ℓp(θ)=n2log⁡[S(θ)/n]+n/2+C\ell_p(\boldsymbol\theta)=\tfrac n2\log[S(\boldsymbol\theta)/n]+n/2+Cℓp​(θ)=2n​log[S(θ)/n]+n/2+C. Profiling the other response parameters as well yields

Dj(c)=nlog⁡ ⁣[S~j(c)S(θ^)].D_j(c)=n\log\!\left[\frac{\widetilde S_j(c)}{S(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}\right].Dj​(c)=nlog[S(θ^)Sj​(c)​].
(31)

This is not [S~j(c)−S(θ^)]/s2[\widetilde S_j(c)-S(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})]/s^2[Sj​(c)−S(θ^)]/s2. The ML variance estimate uses divisor nnn, while the conventional residual estimate uses n−pn-pn−p. A perfect fit S=0S=0S=0 makes the likelihood unbounded as variance tends to zero. The stable loop below assumes known unit variance; changing that assumption requires changing the statistic and its interpretation. See Held & Sabanés Bové, §5.3, pp. 130--131 for profiling a Gaussian variance nuisance parameter.

At fixed parameter 1, a profile refits parameter 2 along the vertical line. A slice keeps parameter 2 fixed. The homothetic ellipses are illustrative quadratic level sets, not the actual BOD likelihood.

def profile_model(observations):
    """BOD negative log likelihood, with shared parameters."""
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()
    m.asymptote = pyo.Var(initialize=theta["asymptote"], bounds=(1e-6, None))
    m.rate_constant = pyo.Var(initialize=theta["rate_constant"], bounds=(1e-6, None))
    m.nll = pyo.Objective(expr=0.5 * sum(
        (row.y - m.asymptote * (1 - pyo.exp(-m.rate_constant * row.time_days)))**2
        for row in observations.itertuples()))
    return m


def profile_parameter(name, grid):
    """Fix one parameter and re-optimize the other at each grid point."""
    m = profile_model(data)
    solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
    solver.options["linear_solver"] = "mumps"
    rows = []
    for value in grid:
        getattr(m, name).fix(float(value))
        pyo.assert_optimal_termination(solver.solve(m))
        rows.append((float(value), 2 * (pyo.value(m.nll) - nll_hat)))
    return np.asarray(rows)


profile_grids = {"asymptote": np.linspace(17, 22, 101),
                 "rate_constant": np.linspace(0.35, 0.8, 101)}
profiles = {name: profile_parameter(name, grid)
            for name, grid in profile_grids.items()}

Proposed ParmEst API (not executed)¶

Pyomo PR #3875 is open and draft as checked October 17, 2026, at head d86863725c676f71a4105c1f72060baa150b4e65. The installed course Pyomo 6.10.1 has no Estimator.profile_likelihood method. This preview requires that development branch and its dependencies and stays disabled here.

At this exact PR head, the method returns (profiles, intervals, theta_hat, obj_hat). For unregularized SSE_weighted, its lr_stat already equals 2 * len(exp_list) * (obj - obj_hat), converting the average objective to the summed likelihood scale. Do not multiply the returned statistic by the experiment count again. The SSE option instead profiles an unknown common variance and uses n_residuals * log(obj / obj_hat). These are different error-scale assumptions. See the pinned implementation.

The figure below is from the explicit stable-Pyomo implementation. The development preview has not been executed.

from scipy.stats import chi2
cutoff = chi2.ppf(0.95, df=1)
for name, curve in profiles.items():
    # Interpolate the two threshold crossings; fail if the grid misses either.
    k = np.argmin(curve[:, 1])
    assert curve[0, 1] > cutoff and curve[-1, 1] > cutoff
    left = np.interp(cutoff, curve[:k+1, 1][::-1], curve[:k+1, 0][::-1])
    right = np.interp(cutoff, curve[k:, 1], curve[k:, 0])
    print(f"{name}: profile 95% interval [{left:.4f}, {right:.4f}]")
    assert curve[k, 1] >= -1e-5
print(f"Likelihood-ratio cutoff (1 parameter): {cutoff:.4f}")

Identifiability depends on the model, designs, and data¶

Global structural identifiability over allowed designs means

[f(φ,θ)=f(φ,θ~) for every allowed φ] ⟹ θ=θ~.[\mathbf f(\boldsymbol\varphi,\boldsymbol\theta) =\mathbf f(\boldsymbol\varphi,\widetilde{\boldsymbol\theta}) \text{ for every allowed }\boldsymbol\varphi] \ \Longrightarrow\ \boldsymbol\theta=\widetilde{\boldsymbol\theta}.[f(φ,θ)=f(φ,θ) for every allowed φ] ⟹ θ=θ.
(32)

It concerns ideal predictions and the parameter domain. Practical identifiability concerns whether finite noisy observations constrain the parameters enough for the intended inference. A flat, one-sided, or unbounded profile can reveal weak practical information even when a local covariance can be computed. See Raue et al. (2009), §2.3, pp. 1924--1925.

At a fixed local fit, Qv=0\mathbf Q\mathbf v=\mathbf0Qv=0 for a nonzero v\mathbf vv implies Mv=0\mathbf M\mathbf v=\mathbf0Mv=0. This direction has no first-order effect on the available predictions. Full local rank does not rule out a different distant parameter vector giving identical predictions. Conversely, singular first-order information at an exceptional point need not prove global nonidentifiability; higher-order changes can matter.

The known-σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 profile intervals below have two threshold crossings. Bates & Watts’ BOD plots, pp. 206--207, use estimated noise and Student ttt calibration: their 95% intervals are much wider, and their 99% intervals have no finite right endpoint. These results concern different inferential assumptions and levels.

def plot_region_comparison(results):

From covariance to experimental design¶

At the fitted parameter and the stated error scale, the analytically checked finite-difference covariance gives the existing-data information Mold=V^−1\mathbf M_{\mathrm{old}}=\widehat{\mathbf V}^{-1}Mold​=V−1. The software name prior_FIM refers to information from previous experiments here; it is not a Bayesian prior distribution.

For one independent new BOD measurement, use the row sensitivity

q(t)=[1−e−θ^2tθ^1te−θ^2t],Mtotal(t)=Mold+q(t)Tq(t)σ2.\mathbf q(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1-e^{-\hat\theta_2t}&\hat\theta_1t e^{-\hat\theta_2t}\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf M_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\mathbf M_{\mathrm{old}}+\frac{\mathbf q(t)^T\mathbf q(t)}{\sigma^2}.q(t)=[1−e−θ^2​t​θ^1​te−θ^2​t​],Mtotal​(t)=Mold​+σ2q(t)Tq(t)​.
(33)

The column vector in the updated_fim implementation below is the transpose of this row; np.outer produces the same 2×22\times22×2 contribution. A scalar observation adds at most rank-one information. Its direction matters as well as the sizes of its sensitivity components.

A local design minimizes a chosen scalar criterion JJJ at a fixed nominal parameter:

min⁡φ∈ΦJ[Mold(θ^)+Mnew(φ,θ^)].\min_{\boldsymbol\varphi\in\Phi} J[\mathbf M_{\mathrm{old}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})+ \mathbf M_{\mathrm{new}}(\boldsymbol\varphi,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})].φ∈Φmin​J[Mold​(θ^)+Mnew​(φ,θ^)].
(34)

For the D-optimal BOD design, maximize log⁡det⁡Mtotal(t)\log\det\mathbf M_{\mathrm{total}}(t)logdetMtotal​(t) on 0.5≤t≤50.5\le t\le50.5≤t≤5 days. The future measured value is unnecessary for choosing this local design; it is needed for the subsequent refit. After measurement, update both the fitted parameters and information. See Bates & Watts, §3.14.4, p. 127; Seber & Wild, §5.13.1, pp. 250--251; Laky et al. (2026), §2.1--2.2.

Independent measurement information adds at the same nominal parameter, coordinate scale and noise model.

q_rate = theta["asymptote"] * t_design * np.exp(-theta["rate_constant"] * t_design)

Optimize the next measurement¶

Pyomo 6.10 configures the objective and solver behavior in the DesignOfExperiments constructor. run_doe() performs the optimization and stores the summary in doe.results.

The bounds in BODExperiment restrict the new measurement to 0.5--5 days.

prior_fim = np.linalg.inv(covariance)
design_experiment = BODExperiment(
    {"time_days": 2.0, "y": 10.0},
    measurement_standard_deviation=1.0,
    theta=dict(theta),
    design_bounds=(0.5, 5.0),
)

# Use the MUMPS linear solver available in the course environment.
ipopt = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
ipopt.options["linear_solver"] = "mumps"

doe = DesignOfExperiments(
    experiment=design_experiment,
    fd_formula="central",
    step=1e-3,
    objective_option=ObjectiveLib.determinant,
    prior_FIM=prior_fim,
    improve_cholesky_roundoff_error=True,
    solver=ipopt,
    tee=False,
)
doe.run_doe(model=doe.create_doe_model())

optimal_time = doe.results["Experiment Design"][0]
print(f"D-optimal next measurement: {optimal_time:.6f} days")
D-optimal next measurement: 1.499740 days

Verify with an independent calculation¶

For this two-parameter model, a dense grid is cheap. It provides an independent check on the software formulation and local optimizer.

def updated_fim(t):
    sensitivity = np.array(
        [
            1 - np.exp(-theta["rate_constant"] * t),
            theta["asymptote"] * t * np.exp(-theta["rate_constant"] * t),
        ]
    )
    return prior_fim + np.outer(sensitivity, sensitivity)


grid = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 2001)
grid_logdet = np.array([np.linalg.slogdet(updated_fim(t))[1] for t in grid])
grid_time = grid[np.argmax(grid_logdet)]

print(f"Dense-grid optimum: {grid_time:.6f} days")
print(f"Prior log determinant:   {np.linalg.slogdet(prior_fim)[1]:.6f}")
print(f"Updated log determinant: {grid_logdet.max():.6f}")
assert abs(optimal_time - grid_time) < 0.02

plt.plot(grid, grid_logdet, color="black")
plt.axvline(optimal_time, color="#D55E00", linestyle="--", label="Pyomo.DoE optimum")
plt.xlabel("Measurement time (days)")
plt.ylabel("Updated log determinant")

Information eigenvalues and design criteria¶

For M=Udiag⁡(λj)UT≻0\mathbf M=\mathbf U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)\mathbf U^T\succ0M=Udiag(λj​)UT≻0, orthogonality gives

tr⁡M=∑jλj,det⁡M=∏jλj,tr⁡M−1=∑jλj−1,κ2(M)=λmax⁡/λmin⁡.\operatorname{tr}\mathbf M=\sum_j\lambda_j,\quad \det\mathbf M=\prod_j\lambda_j,\quad \operatorname{tr}\mathbf M^{-1}=\sum_j\lambda_j^{-1},\quad \kappa_2(\mathbf M)=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}.trM=j∑​λj​,detM=j∏​λj​,trM−1=j∑​λj−1​,κ2​(M)=λmax​/λmin​.
(35)
CriterionObjectiveWhat it controls in the local approximationPyomo.DoE option
AMinimize ∑j1/λj\sum_j1/\lambda_j∑j​1/λj​Sum of parameter variances in the chosen unitstrace
DMaximize ∏jλj\prod_j\lambda_j∏j​λj​Minimize ellipsoid volume at a common cutoffdeterminant
EMaximize λmin⁡\lambda_{\min}λmin​Minimize the largest covariance eigenvalue and longest semi-axisminimum_eigenvalue
MEMinimize λmax⁡/λmin⁡\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}λmax​/λmin​Balance axes; it does not control overall sizecondition_number
pseudo-AMaximize ∑jλj\sum_j\lambda_j∑j​λj​Increase total information; not A-optimalitypseudo_trace

The ellipse’s longest-to-shortest semi-axis ratio is κ2(M)\sqrt{\kappa_2(\mathbf M)}κ2​(M)​, not κ2(M)\kappa_2(\mathbf M)κ2​(M). A-optimality minimizes trace of covariance, not the volume of an enclosing coordinate box. Such a box depends on covariance diagonal entries and its volume involves their product. Pseudo-A is also called a trace or T criterion; a finite trace can coexist with a zero eigenvalue and an unidentifiable direction.

For information eigenvalues (16,1)(16,1)(16,1) and (4,3)(4,3)(4,3), the A objectives are 17/1617/1617/16 and 7/127/127/12; D objectives are 16 and 12; E objectives are 1 and 3; ME objectives are 16 and 4/34/34/3; pseudo-A objectives are 17 and 7. Thus A, E and ME prefer the second design, while D and pseudo-A prefer the first. There is no universal ordering of designs independent of the objective. See Laky et al. (2026), §2.2, Eqs. (12)--(18) and Table 1.

The five curves below use the same original observations, fitted parameters, units, and allowed time interval. Their grid optima need not coincide.

# Evaluate all five criteria on the same time grid and parameter scaling.
criteria_time = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 901)
criteria_information = np.asarray([updated_fim(t) for t in criteria_time])
eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(criteria_information)
assert np.all(eigenvalues > 0)
criteria_values = {
    "A: minimize trace inverse": np.sum(1/eigenvalues, axis=1),
    "D: maximize determinant": np.prod(eigenvalues, axis=1),
    "E: maximize smallest eigenvalue": eigenvalues[:, 0],
    "ME: minimize condition number": eigenvalues[:, 1]/eigenvalues[:, 0],
    "Pseudo-A: maximize trace": np.sum(eigenvalues, axis=1),
}
criteria_results = {"time": criteria_time.tolist(),
    "criteria": {key: value.tolist() for key, value in criteria_values.items()}}

Parameter scaling and Cholesky implementation¶

Let θ=Dη\boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\eta}θ=Dη, where D=diag⁡(s1,…,sp)\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_p)D=diag(s1​,…,sp​) and sj>0s_j>0sj​>0. The chain rule gives Qη=QθD\mathbf{Q}_\eta=\mathbf{Q}_\theta \mathbf{D}Qη​=Qθ​D and Mη=DMθD\mathbf{M}_\eta=\mathbf{D} \mathbf{M}_\theta \mathbf{D}Mη​=DMθ​D. Thus parameter scaling changes the units in which uncertainty is compared and can change A-, E-, ME-, and pseudo-A-optimal designs. D-optimal rankings are unchanged by a fixed nonsingular scaling because det⁡(Mη)=det⁡(D)2det⁡(Mθ)\det(\mathbf{M}_\eta)=\det(\mathbf{D})^2\det(\mathbf{M}_\theta)det(Mη​)=det(D)2det(Mθ​).

Multiplying the entire information matrix by one positive constant does not change its condition number: κ2(cM)=cλmax/(cλmin)=κ2(M)\kappa_2(c\mathbf{M})=c\lambda_{max}/(c\lambda_{min})=\kappa_2(\mathbf{M})κ2​(cM)=cλmax​/(cλmin​)=κ2​(M). scale_constant_value controls a common scale; scale_nominal_param_value multiplies sensitivity columns by their nominal parameter values. Do not confuse these two scaling operations.

For positive-definite M\mathbf{M}M, a Cholesky factorization M=LLT\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{LL}^TM=LLT has Ljj>0L_{jj}>0Ljj​>0 and

det⁡M=(det⁡L)2=(∏jLjj)2,log⁡det⁡M=2∑jlog⁡Ljj.\det \mathbf{M}=(\det \mathbf{L})^2=\left(\prod_j L_{jj}\right)^2,\qquad \log\det \mathbf{M}=2\sum_j\log L_{jj}.detM=(detL)2=(j∏​Ljj​)2,logdetM=2j∑​logLjj​.
(36)

Pyomo.DoE introduces L\mathbf{L}L as variables and M=LLT\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{LL}^TM=LLT as constraints for its smooth log-determinant formulation. Eigenvalue criteria use external calculations and derivatives. See Laky et al. (2026), Section 2 and Table 1.

A nonuniform parameter scaling can improve or worsen the condition number; improvement is not guaranteed. Scale the existing-data information consistently with new-experiment information before adding the matrices.

Why adding information reduces predicted covariance¶

At a fixed nominal parameter, write the new information as ATA⪰0\mathbf A^T\mathbf A\succeq0ATA⪰0 and suppose M0≻0\mathbf M_0\succ0M0​≻0. Let B=AM0−1/2\mathbf B=\mathbf A\mathbf M_0^{-1/2}B=AM0−1/2​. Then

M1=M0+ATA=M01/2(I+BTB)M01/2,M1−1=M0−1/2(I+BTB)−1M0−1/2⪯M0−1.\begin{aligned} \mathbf M_1&=\mathbf M_0+\mathbf A^T\mathbf A =\mathbf M_0^{1/2}(\mathbf I+\mathbf B^T\mathbf B)\mathbf M_0^{1/2},\\ \mathbf M_1^{-1} &=\mathbf M_0^{-1/2}(\mathbf I+\mathbf B^T\mathbf B)^{-1}\mathbf M_0^{-1/2} \preceq\mathbf M_0^{-1}. \end{aligned}M1​M1−1​​=M0​+ATA=M01/2​(I+BTB)M01/2​,=M0−1/2​(I+BTB)−1M0−1/2​⪯M0−1​.​
(37)

The eigenvalues of (I+BTB)−1(\mathbf I+\mathbf B^T\mathbf B)^{-1}(I+BTB)−1 lie in (0,1](0,1](0,1], so predicted variance cannot increase in any fixed direction. Equality may remain in directions the new experiment does not inform. Recomputing sensitivities at a different refitted parameter changes the premise: an observed covariance need not match this fixed-parameter prediction.

For one scalar measurement, set u=qT/σ\mathbf u=\mathbf q^T/\sigmau=qT/σ and use the rank-one formulas

det⁡(M0+uuT)det⁡M0=1+uTM0−1u,(M0+uuT)−1=M0−1−M0−1uuTM0−11+uTM0−1u.\frac{\det(\mathbf M_0+\mathbf u\mathbf u^T)}{\det\mathbf M_0} =1+\mathbf u^T\mathbf M_0^{-1}\mathbf u, \qquad (\mathbf M_0+\mathbf u\mathbf u^T)^{-1} =\mathbf M_0^{-1} -\frac{\mathbf M_0^{-1}\mathbf u\mathbf u^T\mathbf M_0^{-1}} {1+\mathbf u^T\mathbf M_0^{-1}\mathbf u}.detM0​det(M0​+uuT)​=1+uTM0−1​u,(M0​+uuT)−1=M0−1​−1+uTM0−1​uM0−1​uuTM0−1​​.
(38)

The D-optimal next measurement therefore maximizes its sensitivity in the existing covariance metric, qV^qT/σ2\mathbf q\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf q^T/\sigma^2qVqT/σ2. Merely choosing the largest Euclidean sensitivity norm ignores information already collected. These identities apply to the local additive-information model used here; they are not guarantees about the realized refit.

Close the loop: take the designed measurement¶

The design step produced a time, not data. Closing the loop means going back to the experiment, measuring at t⋆t^\start⋆, appending the result, and re-estimating.

This is exactly where the digital experiment is needed: we evaluate the true response at t⋆t^\start⋆, add one noise draw, and hand the seven-point data set back to parmest.

The quantity to watch is det⁡Vθ\det\mathbf{V}_\thetadetVθ​. Because the 95% confidence region is the ellipse

(θ−θ^)TVθ−1(θ−θ^)≤χ2,0.952=5.991,(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{V}_\theta^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\le\chi^2_{2,0.95}=5.991,(θ−θ^)TVθ−1​(θ−θ^)≤χ2,0.952​=5.991,
(39)

its area is π χ2,0.952det⁡Vθ\pi\,\chi^2_{2,0.95}\sqrt{\det\mathbf{V}_\theta}πχ2,0.952​detVθ​​. A smaller determinant is a smaller ellipse, and D-optimal design maximizes det⁡F\det\mathbf{F}detF, which is the same objective seen from the other side.

CHI2_95_2DOF = 5.991  # 95% quantile of the chi-squared distribution, 2 degrees of freedom


def ellipse_area(cov):
    """Area of the 95% confidence ellipse implied by a 2x2 covariance matrix."""
    return np.pi * CHI2_95_2DOF * np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(cov))


def summarize(label, theta, cov):
    """One row of the before/after comparison table."""
    sd = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
    return {
        "design": label,
        "theta_1": theta["asymptote"],
        "theta_2": theta["rate_constant"],
        "sd(theta_1)": sd[0],
        "sd(theta_2)": sd[1],
        "det(V)": np.linalg.det(cov),
        "ellipse area": ellipse_area(cov),
    }

def plot_sequential_regions(results):
    """Separate the actual estimate shift from the change in ellipse shape."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
    angles = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 361)
    circle = np.vstack([np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)])
    before = np.array([results["before_theta"]["asymptote"], results["before_theta"]["rate_constant"]])
    after = np.array([results["after_theta"]["asymptote"], results["after_theta"]["rate_constant"]])
    for ax, centered in zip(axes, [False, True]):
        for center, cov, style, color, label in [
            (before, results["before_cov"], "--", "#D55E00", "6 observations"),
            (after, results["after_cov"], "-", "#0072B2", "7 observations")]:
            values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(np.asarray(cov))
            shown_center = before if centered else center
            points = shown_center[:, None] + vectors @ (np.sqrt(results["cutoff"]*values)[:, None]*circle)
            ax.plot(*points, ls=style, color=color, label=label)
            ax.plot(*shown_center, marker="x" if label.startswith("6") else "+", color=color, ms=8)
        ax.set(xlabel=r"$\theta_1$ (mg/L)", ylabel=r"$\theta_2$ (day$^{-1}$)",
               title="Centers aligned: shape comparison" if centered else "Actual estimates and regions")
        ax.legend(fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

A control: was the design step worth it?¶

A shrinking ellipse is not by itself evidence that the design helped. Any seventh observation adds information. The question is whether t⋆t^\start⋆ adds more than a time we could have picked without optimizing.

Two controls, both inside the same 0.5--5 day window:

  • t=0.5t=0.5t=0.5 days, the time the dense grid identified as the worst in the window; and

  • t=5t=5t=5 days, the naive “measure at the end” choice.

Each control uses its own noise draw, so the three augmented data sets differ in the new point only.

One realization is not evidence¶

The table above compares three single draws. That is a weak comparison: Vθ\mathbf{V}_\thetaVθ​ from the Gauss–Newton calculation depends on sensitivities at the refitted parameters as well as on where the measurement was placed, so a lucky draw at the worst time can beat an unlucky draw at t⋆t^\start⋆.

The Fisher information prediction has no such noise in it. To check that the prediction is the right summary of what actually happens, repeat each placement over many noise draws and average the realized det⁡Vθ\det\mathbf{V}_\thetadetVθ​.

All three placements share the same standardized draws -- common random numbers -- so the comparison is between times, not between lucky and unlucky noise.

standardized_draws = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(0.0, 1.0, REPLICATES)

for label, t_new in candidates.items():
    determinants = []
    for z in standardized_draws:
        y_new = float(bod_response(t_new, THETA_TRUE) + MEASUREMENT_STD * z)
        trial = pd.concat(
            [data, pd.DataFrame({"time_days": [t_new], "y": [y_new]})], ignore_index=True
        )
        determinants.append(np.linalg.det(estimate_parameters(trial)[2]))

    determinants = np.array(determinants)
    study.append(
        {
            "design": label,
            "mean det(V)": determinants.mean(),
            "mean reduction": 1 - determinants.mean() / np.linalg.det(covariance),
            "predicted reduction": 1
            - np.linalg.det(np.linalg.inv(updated_fim(t_new))) / np.linalg.det(covariance),
        }
    )

def confidence_ellipse(center, cov, n_points=200):
    """Points on the 95% confidence ellipse of a 2x2 covariance matrix."""
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    angle = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_points)
    unit_circle = np.vstack([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)])
    radii = np.sqrt(CHI2_95_2DOF * eigenvalues)
    return (eigenvectors @ (radii[:, None] * unit_circle)).T + np.array(center)

# its own center, but overlaying them there would mix a change in shape with a
# change in location; only the shape is what the design step controls.

    (realized_covariance[optimal_label], "--", f"+ {optimal_label}"),
]

for cov, style, label in ellipses:
    points = confidence_ellipse(center, cov)
    plt.plot(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], linestyle=style, label=label)

plt.scatter(*center, color="black", zorder=3)
plt.xlabel(r"$\theta_1$ (asymptote)")

plt.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()

The D-optimal design minimizes the determinant of the predicted covariance, hence the area of this two-parameter ellipse. It does not specifically minimize the longest axis (the E-optimal criterion). Adding positive-semidefinite information at the same nominal parameters cannot increase variance in any fixed direction; re-estimating the parameters after collecting data can also change the sensitivities and rotate the ellipse.

Extensions and further reading¶

The BOD calculation holds the response model, noise distribution, and known noise scale fixed. The following extensions change specific parts of that formulation.

ExtensionWhat changesStarting point
Errors in variablesModel uncertainty in measured inputs as well as outputs; latent true inputs can become estimation variables.Britt & Luecke (1973), DOI; Seber & Wild, §1.4
Correlated errorsUse a joint likelihood/covariance; the scalar error suffix does not encode off-diagonal terms.White & Domowitz (1984), Nonlinear Regression with Dependent Observations; Bates & Watts, §3.8; Seber & Wild, Chapter 6
Bootstrap refinementsChoose residual, case, bias-corrected, or other intervals to match the sampling assumptions; assess simulation error.Wehrens et al. (2000), DOI; Boos & Stefanski (2013), §11.5
Small-sample likelihood calibrationBartlett-type corrections can reduce chi-squared calibration error under their model-specific regularity and expansion conditions.Cordeiro & Cribari-Neto (2014), §2.4, pp. 20--23
Profile likelihoodRefit nuisance parameters to inspect asymmetry and one-sided or unbounded intervals.Raue et al. (2009), DOI
Regularized estimationAdd a penalty and examine bias as well as variance; penalized curvature is not automatically frequentist sampling information.Hoerl & Kennard (1970), Theorem 4.3, p. 62, DOI
Sparse estimation and priorsAn L1L_1L1​ penalty can set coefficients to zero; the choice depends on the model and sparsity assumptions.Tibshirani (1996), §5 and §11; Park & Casella (2008), DOI
Uncertain parameters in designAverage utility over parameter uncertainty or protect against a specified uncertainty set.Chaloner & Verdinelli (1995), article; Seber & Wild, §5.13.2
Continuous effortOptimize nonnegative weights over candidate experiments, then convert weights into a finite allocation.Pukelsheim (2006), §9.4 and §12.4--12.5; Kiefer & Wolfowitz (1960), DOI
Model discriminationChoose measurements that distinguish competing response models, rather than only refining parameters of one model.Buzzi-Ferraris & Forzatti (1983), DOI; Seber & Wild, §5.13.5
Multiresponse estimationEstimate a common unknown error covariance for several outputs; profiling it can yield a determinant-based fitting objective.Bates & Watts, Chapter 4, pp. 134--140
Black-box informationApproximate information from likelihood evaluations when derivative access is limited.Spall (2005), DOI
Dynamic applicationsInclude trajectories, constraints, and hardware validation in model building and design.Franceschini & Macchietto (2008), DOI; Wilson et al. (2014); Bandara et al. (2009)

For a Gaussian prior with precision P\mathbf PP and mean μ\boldsymbol\muμ, MAP estimation adds 12(θ−μ)TP(θ−μ)\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\theta-\boldsymbol\mu)^T\mathbf P(\boldsymbol\theta-\boldsymbol\mu)21​(θ−μ)TP(θ−μ) to the negative log likelihood. Its Hessian contributes P\mathbf PP to local posterior curvature. Ridge theory can establish a bias--variance tradeoff in specified linear models; it does not guarantee a large variance reduction for an arbitrary nonlinear BOD fit. An L1L_1L1​ penalty corresponds to independent Laplace priors for MAP estimation, while Bayesian posterior sampling is a different operation.

The ParmEst tutorial and Pyomo.DoE tutorial retain the larger dynamic-model implementations. Classical factorial designs, blocking, and response surfaces address additional experimental-design questions; see Dean, Voss & Draguljić (2017), Chapters on factorial, block, and response-surface designs. An information-based design for one fixed model does not replace those methods.

Carry remaining uncertainty into decisions¶

Stopping the measurement loop depends on prediction needs and experimental budget. Bootstrap parameter draws can support scenario construction if their sampling interpretation is suitable for the decision task. A confidence region alone supplies no scenario probabilities. Stochastic programming develops decisions under specified scenarios and probabilities.

Key takeaways¶

  • Parameter estimation turns measurements into fitted parameters and an uncertainty description.

  • The inverse Gauss–Newton covariance supplies local prior information for the next design.

  • Experimental design asks where a new measurement adds information not already supplied by the prior.

  • A design is only a prediction. Closing the loop -- taking the measurement and re-estimating -- is what tests it, and a digital experiment makes that possible when the real apparatus is gone.

  • Check the design against a control. That a seventh observation shrinks the confidence region proves nothing on its own; the comparison that matters is against a measurement placed without optimizing.

  • A single realization is a weak comparison, because the estimated covariance changes with the refitted parameters. Average over draws, or compare the noise-free Fisher information prediction.

  • FIM designs are local: different nominal parameters, noise models, bounds, or priors can change the answer.

  • Small examples permit independent checks. Use them before trusting a larger dynamic design.
